prompt.context_jp: 薬が効いて 容体も落ち着いたようで よかったです 実は 今日 機長のラストフライトでして
prompt.prompt_jp: 薬___効いて 容体も落ち着いたようで よかったです
prompt.prompt_en: Choose the particle that fits here.

feedback.correct_en: The medicine is being newly introduced as the thing that is working — new information about a specific subject in a subordinate clause, so が is natural.
feedback.incorrect_en: は would topicalize 'the medicine' as something already under discussion, which doesn't fit this reporting-of-a-fact clause.

contrast_examples.en: That medicine (as for it) doesn't work. (topic/contrast)

prompt.context_jp: そのとおりだ それなのに さっきは何だ？
prompt.prompt_jp: さっき___何だ？

feedback.correct_en: The captain is contrasting Fukazawa's usual bravado with his earlier panic — 'as for a moment ago' (contrastive topic), so は fits.
feedback.incorrect_en: が would mark 'a moment ago' as new subject information, which doesn't match this scolding, contrastive tone.

contrast_examples.jp: さっきは失礼しました。

prompt.context_jp: 相変わらず 口だけは達者だな
prompt.prompt_jp: 相変わらず 口だけ___達者だな

feedback.correct_en: '口だけは' sets up an implicit contrast — 'your mouth, at least, is sharp (but not the rest).' は after だけ gives the characteristic contrastive 'only X (but not others)' nuance.
feedback.incorrect_en: が wouldn't carry that implicit contrast with other skills; the sentence loses its sarcastic bite.

contrast_examples.en: His looks, at least, are good (implying nothing else is).

prompt.context_jp: 今 副操縦士の深澤が 1人で操縦してます
prompt.prompt_jp: 今 副操縦士の深澤___1人で操縦してます

feedback.correct_en: Fukazawa is being newly identified as the one currently flying — this is new-information が answering the implicit question 'who is flying?'
feedback.incorrect_en: は would frame Fukazawa as an already-established topic, but here he's being introduced as the agent in this emergency explanation.

contrast_examples.en: Fukazawa (of all people) is flying. (new info)

prompt.context_jp: どうして 俺が ラストフライトのコーパイに お前を指名したか分かるか？
prompt.prompt_jp: どうして 俺___ラストフライトのコーパイに お前を指名したか分かるか？

feedback.correct_en: In embedded wh-questions like 'why I chose you,' the subject takes が. It also emphasizes 'I (of all people)' as the one who made the choice.
feedback.incorrect_en: は inside a subordinate clause with a wh-word sounds unnatural here; the captain is focusing on the act of choosing, not setting himself up as topic.

prompt.context_jp: やっぱり 右耳が聞こえづらいらしくて
prompt.prompt_jp: やっぱり 右耳___聞こえづらいらしくて

feedback.correct_en: With adjectives like 聞こえづらい describing a body part's state, が marks the specific thing that's affected — 'his right ear is hard to hear with.'
feedback.incorrect_en: は would suggest contrast ('the right ear, in contrast with the left'), which isn't the point here — Hirose is reporting the newly confirmed fact.

contrast_examples.en: The right ear (unlike the left) is fine.

prompt.context_jp: 生まれた時から この病院のお嬢様なんて
prompt.prompt_jp: 生まれた時から この病院のお嬢様なんて 人生勝ち組___いいとこだよな

feedback.correct_en: The set phrase '〜もいいところだ' means 'that's a prime example of X' — fixed with も.
feedback.incorrect_en: が breaks the idiomatic construction; the speaker is labeling her life as a textbook case of being on the winning side.

prompt.context_jp: 娘と こんなやりとりが できる日が来るなんて 思いもしなかったよ
prompt.prompt_jp: 全部 君のおかげだよ。改めて ホント___ありがとう

feedback.correct_en: 'ホントにありがとう' uses に to turn ホント into an adverb modifying ありがとう — 'truly thank you.'
feedback.incorrect_en: が would mark ホント as a subject, which makes no sense in this adverbial expression.

prompt.context_jp: 必ず 誰よりも うまくなって
prompt.prompt_jp: この手で 多くの人___救ってみせます

feedback.correct_en: 救う takes a direct object marked by を — 'save many people.'
feedback.incorrect_en: に would turn 'many people' into a destination/recipient, which doesn't match 救う's transitive argument structure.

prompt.context_jp: 立場とか場所とかじゃなく 何をするか なんじゃないかなって
prompt.prompt_jp: 大事なの___立場とか場所とかじゃなく 何をするか なんじゃないかな

feedback.correct_en: '大事なのは〜' sets up 'the important thing' as the topic of the whole statement — classic topic-comment structure.
feedback.incorrect_en: が would make it sound like identifying 'which thing is important' out of options, but she's stating a general principle, so は is natural.

prompt.context_jp: 耳鳴り。あと おそらく 難聴も
prompt.prompt_jp: どっちもさ 右側だけってのが 気になってて
prompt.prompt_en: Pick the particle for: 右側___ってのが気になって

feedback.correct_en: '右側だけ' ('only the right side') captures the anomaly — the problem is confined to one side, which is clinically suspicious.
feedback.incorrect_en: こそ would mean 'the right side above all,' which doesn't convey the 'only' limitation that makes the symptom notable.

prompt.context_jp: わずかですが 無血管野が見られます
prompt.prompt_jp: おそらく 機長___肺塞栓症です

feedback.correct_en: The captain is the established topic of discussion (他に話題はない); Iori is giving a diagnosis 'about the captain,' so は fits the 'X is Y' topic-comment pattern.
feedback.incorrect_en: が would make it sound like identifying who has PE out of several patients, but there's only one patient under discussion.

contrast_examples.en: The captain has pulmonary embolism. (describing topic)

prompt.context_jp: サチュレーションが 下がってます
prompt.prompt_jp: このままでは 心停止の恐れ___あります

feedback.correct_en: '〜恐れがある' ('there is a risk of〜') is a fixed existential pattern that uses が with ある.
feedback.incorrect_en: は would strangely topicalize 'the risk' as if already known; here the risk is being newly raised as the concern.

prompt.context_jp: 良性な腫瘍ではありますが
prompt.prompt_jp: これ___小脳を圧迫し 耳鳴りや目まい 体に倦怠感などの症状を 引き起こしている

feedback.correct_en: In a 〜が…し、…引き起こす subordinate clause explaining cause, が marks 'this (tumor)' as the agent doing the compressing.
feedback.incorrect_en: は would break the subordinate clause structure and oddly topicalize 'this' mid-explanation.

prompt.context_jp: 聴神経腫瘍は 初期症状が 突発性難聴などと 酷似しているため
prompt.prompt_jp: 聴神経腫瘍___初期症状が 突発性難聴などと 酷似している

feedback.correct_en: Classic double-subject construction: 聴神経腫瘍は (topic, 'as for acoustic neuroma') + 初期症状が (inner subject, 'its early symptoms'). The outer frame uses は.
feedback.incorrect_en: Using が on both would create two competing subjects with no topic framing — the explanation loses its 'about X: Y is Z' structure.

contrast_examples.en: Elephants have long trunks. (topic + inner subject)

prompt.context_jp: 呼吸苦を軽く見てはならぬという直感が、
prompt.prompt_jp: 直感___彼の内で鳴っていた

feedback.correct_en: The intuition is newly introduced as a thing that was 'sounding' inside him — narrative description of an event, so が.
feedback.incorrect_en: は would presume 直感 is already a known topic; here it's being presented freshly as the force acting on him.

prompt.context_jp: 機長には 大変 お世話になったので
prompt.prompt_jp: ___に 最高のフライト プレゼントしたいって みんなで話してた

feedback.correct_en: はなむけ ('parting gift / send-off') is the set word for a farewell tribute to someone retiring or departing.
feedback.incorrect_en: みやげ is a souvenir from a trip; かたみ is a memento of the deceased. Neither fits a retirement send-off.

prompt.context_jp: (Tsujimura quoting Goethe)
prompt.prompt_jp: 女心と___空は そっくりだっていうよ

feedback.correct_en: The proverb is '女心と秋の空' — a woman's heart is as changeable as the autumn sky (fickle, quick to shift).
feedback.incorrect_en: 春の空 and 冬の空 aren't part of this fixed saying; autumn is the traditional image of changeable weather.

contrast_examples.en: A man's heart is like the autumn sky (older variant).

contrast_examples.jp: 秋の空は変わりやすい。

prompt.context_jp: 命の危険が
prompt.prompt_jp: ___しもあらず
prompt.prompt_en: Complete the classical expression meaning 'not entirely absent / cannot be ruled out.'

feedback.correct_en: 'なきにしもあらず' is a classical fixed phrase using the attributive form なき (= ない) — meaning 'not nonexistent / possibly present.'
feedback.incorrect_en: ないに/なくに aren't valid classical forms in this frozen expression.

contrast_examples.jp: 可能性がなきにしもあらず。
望みはなきにしもあらずだ。
contrast_examples.en: There is some hope, if faint.

prompt.context_jp: 頸静脈が怒張してます
prompt.prompt_jp: 一刻を___ます すぐに処置をしないと

feedback.correct_en: '一刻を争う' is the standard medical/emergency idiom meaning 'every moment counts / it's a race against time.'
feedback.incorrect_en: 急ぐ and 待つ don't form the set idiom; 争う is locked in with 一刻を.

contrast_examples.en: It's a situation where every second counts.

prompt.context_jp: ご協力 ありがとうございました
prompt.prompt_jp: いえ ___です

feedback.correct_en: 'とんでもないです' is the standard polite deflection meaning 'not at all / don't mention it' when thanked.
feedback.incorrect_en: もったいない means 'undeserved/wasteful' (used for compliments, not thanks); つまらない is for giving small gifts, not replying to thanks.

contrast_examples.jp: いえ、とんでもないです。
つまらないものですが。
contrast_examples.en: It's just a trifle (when giving a gift).

prompt.context_jp: 俺が せっかく お前の雑用 引き受けてやったのによ
prompt.prompt_jp: お前 ホント ___な

feedback.correct_en: 'ダメちん' — Nokishita's playful insult meaning 'hopeless one' — fits his teasing tone that she couldn't figure out the right question.
feedback.incorrect_en: The other suffixed forms aren't what's spoken here; context is about being ineffective (ダメ), not stupid or unskilled specifically.

prompt.context_jp: 血液を___する薬です
prompt.prompt_jp: 血液を ___する薬

feedback.correct_en: 'サラサラ' describes something flowing smoothly/thinly — the standard way to describe blood-thinning in casual Japanese medical speech.
feedback.incorrect_en: キラキラ means 'sparkling'; ツルツル means 'smooth/slippery (surface).' Neither describes blood viscosity.

contrast_examples.jp: 血液をサラサラにする。

contrast_examples.en: The hair is smooth and silky.

prompt.context_jp: Tsujimura dismissing Iori as 'just a technician.'
prompt.prompt_en: Which line fits Tsujimura's cold, superior tone in the story?

choices.text: 医者同士の相談 技師さんは 技師としての 仕事を続けてください
医者同士の相談だから、技師さんも一緒に来てくれる？

feedback.correct_en: Option A is the story line — polite form but dismissive, telling Iori to stay in his lane. The '〜てください' framing is coldly formal.
feedback.incorrect_en: Option B is friendly and inclusive, which contradicts Tsujimura's calculated attempt to exclude Iori from the consultation.

contrast_examples.jp: 仕事を続けてください。

prompt.context_jp: Iori's response when told the drug isn't available.
prompt.prompt_en: Which phrasing is more natural as Iori's calm-but-determined response?

choices.text: ないなら 探しましょう
ないので 探しましょう

feedback.correct_en: 〜なら frames it as 'if (it's the case that) there isn't any, then let's look' — responding to the just-made claim, which is exactly the discourse move here.
feedback.incorrect_en: 〜ので states a reason as fact ('because there isn't, let's look'), which sounds like Iori is agreeing it's absent rather than pushing back on Kurokawa's assumption.

contrast_examples.jp: 時間がないなら急ごう。
contrast_examples.en: If there's no time, let's hurry.
We're hurrying because there's no time.

prompt.context_jp: Onodera reassuring An before the IVR procedure.
prompt.prompt_en: Which sounds more natural as supportive team speech?

choices.text: 大丈夫です 僕たちを信じてください
大丈夫です 僕たちが信じられてください

feedback.correct_en: '僕たちを信じてください' uses the active transitive request — 'please trust us,' natural and warm.
feedback.incorrect_en: Option B mangles passive/causative morphology and isn't grammatical Japanese.

prompt.context_jp: An's cold instruction to the technicians.
prompt.prompt_en: Which version matches An's tone of distancing authority?

choices.text: 技師の方は 医者の指示に従って マニュアルどおり 検査だけ 行っていてください
技師の皆さん、お医者さんの言うとおりに検査してもらえたらうれしいです

feedback.correct_en: Option A is formal, impersonal, and uses '〜だけ' to restrict the technicians to a narrow role — matching An's cold, boundary-drawing tone.
feedback.incorrect_en: Option B is softer and more collegial ('I'd be glad if...'), which contradicts the frosty superiority An is projecting in this scene.

contrast_examples.jp: 〜してもらえたらうれしいです。
contrast_examples.en: I'd be glad if you'd do X. (soft request)

prompt.context_jp: Flight attendant announcement asking passengers for medicine.
prompt.prompt_en: Which phrasing is natural for an in-flight announcement?

choices.text: お客様の中に お持ちの方は いらっしゃいませんか？
お客さんの中で 持ってる人は いないですか？

feedback.correct_en: Option A uses 尊敬語 (お持ちの方, いらっしゃる) — the honorific register required for airline announcements to passengers.
feedback.incorrect_en: Option B is casual/plain and would sound unprofessional over a cabin PA in Japanese service culture.

contrast_examples.jp: お持ちの方はいらっしゃいませんか。
contrast_examples.en: Is there anyone who happens to have one? (honorific)
